title: Mock 3
description: Wider signed conversions, byte stores, loops and byte counting.

questions.title: Architecture and numeric representation

parts.label: A modified Harvard design typically combines…
parts.answer: separate instruction/data caches with unified main memory
options: one register for every memory address
separate instruction/data caches with unified main memory
separate instruction/data main memories with no shared memory

parts.label: Which decimal fraction has a finite binary expansion?

questions.why: Modified Harvard commonly separates instruction/data caches while sharing main memory. 0.625=5/8=.101₂ terminates because its reduced denominator is a power of two.

questions.title: Decode a positive float
questions.prompt: Decode the normal IEEE 754 binary32 representation 0x42160000.
questions.why: The fields are 0 | 10000100 | 00101100000000000000000. Exponent 132−127=5, significand 1.001011₂. Scaling yields 100101.1₂=37.5.

questions.title: Boolean identities
questions.prompt: A prime means NOT; + means OR; juxtaposition means AND. Identify the valid identity in each part.
questions.why: OR distributes over AND in Boolean algebra. Complementing twice restores A. Zero is the identity element for OR.

questions.title: Three-variable K-map
questions.prompt:
Find a minimal sum of products. Columns BC use Gray-code order. Use ASCII primes, no spaces or AND dots, and alphabetical variables within each term.
Output F
A / BC00011110
00011
10001
questions.why: Row A=0, columns 11 and 10 give A'B. Column 10 in both rows gives BC'. Both pairs are needed to cover the two outer 1s; they overlap at A=0, BC=10.

questions.title: Four-variable K-map
questions.prompt:
Find a minimal sum of products. Both axes use Gray-code order. Use ASCII primes, no spaces or AND dots, and alphabetical variables within each term.
Output F
AB / CD00011110
000011
010111
110110
100000
questions.why: Rows 00 and 01, columns 11 and 10 form the group A'C. Rows 01 and 11, columns 01 and 11 form the group BD. These two overlapping groups cover every 1.

questions.title: ARM storage and flags
questions.prompt: Assume ARMv7 A32, 32-bit registers and four-byte words throughout this section.

parts.label: Which register does str r5, [r6, #4] overwrite?
After cmp r1, r2, beq tests…

questions.why: The offset str writes memory at r6+4 and leaves both registers unchanged. beq depends only on the zero flag being set.

questions.title: Place four bytes
questions.prompt: Store the 32-bit word 0xD42A70B9 starting at address 0x0080. Memory is byte-addressable. Drag a chip or choose from the dropdown. The endian cases are independent; options may be reused.
questions.why: Little-endian ascending bytes are B9 70 2A D4. Big-endian ascending bytes are D4 2A 70 B9. Endianness changes byte placement, not bits within each byte.

questions.title: Sequential bitwise trace
questions.prompt:
mov r0, #0x69
mov r1, #0x3c
eor r2, r0, r1
orr r3, r2, #0x80
and r4, r3, #0x5f
Enter 0x followed by exactly 8 hex digits. Later instructions use the earlier results.
questions.why: 69 XOR 3C=55. OR with 80 sets the top bit of the low byte, giving D5. D5 AND 5F=55. Upper 24 bits are zero throughout.

questions.title: One-line C translations
questions.prompt: Variables map to the registers of the same name. Write one lowercase ARM instruction per part. Use explicit three-operand arithmetic.
questions.why: Use add for addition, and with immediate #15 to retain the lowest four bits, and lsl #4 to shift left four positions. The stored shift result is limited to 32 bits.

questions.title: Complete a while loop
questions.why: Exit when r1≥10, so use bge. Increment by 2 and return to the test. The executed values are 2,4,6,8, giving final r0=20 and r1=10.

questions.title: Trace a comparison result
questions.prompt:
Treat r1 and r2 as signed 32-bit integers. Execution ends at done. 
mov r0, #0
cmp r1, r2
beq done
mov r0, #1
bgt done
mov r0, #2
done:

parts.label: Final r0 when r1=−5 and r2=−8 (decimal)
Final r0 when r1=4 and r2=9 (decimal)
Purpose
parts.answer: encode equal as 0, greater as 1, less as 2
options: encode equal as 0, greater as 1, less as 2
encode equal as 0, greater as 2, less as 1

questions.why: Equal inputs branch with r0=0. Unequal inputs set r0=1. bgt retains that for r1>r2; otherwise r0 becomes 2. The mov instructions do not update flags, so bgt still uses cmp.

questions.title: Store a byte, then reload
questions.prompt:
Assume little endian, four-byte words and aligned data. Enter each result as 0x plus exactly 8 hex digits. 
.data
.balign 4
item: .word 0x11223344
.text
ldr r0, =item
mov r1, #0xaa
strb r1, [r0, #2]
ldr r2, [r0]
ldrsb r3, [r0, #2]
questions.why: Original ascending bytes are 44 33 22 11. strb replaces just offset 2: 44 33 AA 11. The word becomes 11AA3344. Loading AA as a signed byte sign-extends its top bit to give FFFFFFAA (−86).

questions.title: Match conditional arithmetic
questions.prompt:
Choose the signed C block with the same behaviour. No arithmetic overflow occurs. Execution ends at done. 
cmp r2, r3
blt smaller
sub r0, r2, r3
b done
smaller:
add r0, r2, r3
done:

parts.label: Equivalent C
parts.answer: if (r2 < r3) r0 = r2 + r3; else r0 = r2 - r3;
options: if (r2 <= r3) r0 = r2 + r3; else r0 = r2 - r3;
if (r2 > r3) r0 = r2 + r3; else r0 = r2 - r3;
if (r2 < r3) r0 = r2 + r3; else r0 = r2 - r3;

questions.why: blt chooses addition only for signed r2<r3. Equality follows the subtraction path, which distinguishes < from <= in the options.

questions.title: Complete a byte-counting program
questions.prompt:
The program counts nonzero bytes in the four-byte array. Complete the missing instruction so it matches the C test shown. Type one lowercase instruction. Execution ends at done. 
// for each of the four bytes:
// if (bytes[i] == 0) skip incrementing the count;
.data
bytes: .byte 0, 5, 0, 9
.text
ldr r4, =bytes
mov r0, #0
mov r1, #0
loop:
ldrb r2, [r4, r1]
cmp r2, #0
[missing instruction]
add r0, r0, #1
skip:
add r1, r1, #1
cmp r1, #4
bne loop
done:
questions.why: beq skip bypasses the count increment for a zero byte. Only 5 and 9 increment r0, giving 2. The index increment occurs on both paths, and the loop stops at r1=4. Byte-array indexing needs no ×4 scaling.
